It is easier to fix a presentation's structure after Copilot has made all the slides.
If your name is on the document, you are responsible for what it says.

blocks.question: Copilot's slide says "Training completion reached 94%", but your source file says 84%. What do you do?
options: Keep it, since Copilot read your files.
Correct it from the file, then check the other figures on that slide too.
Ask Copilot whether it is sure.

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Copilot to draft a document or presentation outline from your own files. Use made-up file names and details.

rubric.description: Says which files or notes the draft must be based on.
States who reads it and asks for a length, outline or structure.
Tells Copilot to use only the sources and mark gaps, and says what you will check.

lessons.goal: Get formulas explained or written, analyze a table and spot trends, then spot-check the results against the data.
lessons.title: Excel: formulas and data

blocks.title: Formulas in plain words
blocks.body: Ask Copilot to explain an inherited formula step by step. Or describe what you need: "Total the amounts in column C where column A is North and column B is March." Naming columns and conditions gives a formula you can test on rows you can calculate by hand.

blocks.title: Analyze a table
blocks.body: Copilot can summarize a table and point out trends and unusual values. Keep your data in a clear table with headers. Ask a specific question: "Which three products grew fastest from January to June?" Work on a copy for changes.

blocks.title: Spot-check the answer
blocks.body: Analysis can skip rows or misread a column. Check the row count, recalculate one total yourself and look at the highest and lowest values. For personal data such as salaries, follow your company's rules.

blocks.question: Copilot misreads your order list, which has blank rows, merged headers and typed subtotals. What is the best first step?
options: Ask the same question with more words.
Tidy it into one plain table with a single header row.
Delete the rows that look unusual.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Copilot says the North region total is 48,200 from 90 rows. Which checks make sense?
options: Count the North rows in your table and compare with 90
Filter to North and add up the amounts yourself
Look at the largest and smallest North amounts for an extra zero
Accept it, since Copilot works from your own workbook

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best completes this request.
blocks.prompt: Explain the formula in cell E2. ___ Then show me how to test it on two rows.
options: Make it simple.
Go through it step by step and say what each part refers to.
Fix it.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A trend Copilot reports should be confirmed against the numbers in your table.
Blank cells and mixed formats in a table never affect an analysis.
If a formula returns a number, it must be correct.

blocks.question: Copilot added a column with a new formula, and the totals look believable. What is the safest next step?
options: Send the sheet, since the totals look believable.
Test it on two or three rows you can calculate by hand.
Ask Copilot whether it is sure.

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Copilot about a table from your work, and describe how you would check the answer. Use made-up data only.

rubric.description: Names the columns and what each one contains.
Says exactly which formula, total or trend is needed.
Names a concrete check such as a row count, a manual total or the highest and lowest values.

courses.title: Research with Sources
courses.description: Research a topic with AI, check every source it gives you and write a short brief where each claim can be traced to a real source.

lessons.goal: Ask an AI search assistant for a sourced answer and confirm that each citation exists and supports the claim.
lessons.title: Check the sources behind an AI answer

blocks.title: Ask for sources
blocks.body: AI search assistants look up web pages and link them in the answer. Ask a narrow question and request a source for every claim, like "What does the regulator say about data retention for small employers?"

blocks.title: Three ways a citation fails
blocks.body: The link may not exist. The page may not contain the claim. Or it says something close, such as another year or country. A link proves nothing until you open it.

blocks.title: Check in three steps
blocks.body: Open the link. Find the sentence the answer relies on. Compare numbers, dates and conditions word by word. Prefer the original source over a blog repeating it.

blocks.question: An AI search answer says a survey found 62% of employees prefer hybrid work, with a link. What do you do first?
options: Trust it, because a link is attached.
Open the link and find the 62% on the page.
Ask the assistant if the number is correct.
Check that the website looks professional.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which are ways a citation can fail?
options: The link leads to a page that does not exist.
The page exists but never mentions the claim.
The page covers a different year than the answer states.
The link opens a page from a well-known organization.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this question most useful for research.
blocks.prompt: What are the notice rules for ending a fixed-term lease in my country? ___
options: Answer briefly.
Give a link for each rule and say which page section it comes from.
Be confident.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A citation can look real and still not support the claim.
If the link opens, the claim is confirmed.
An original source is better than a blog repeating it.
Asking "are you sure?" checks a source.

blocks.question: The answer says "the fee is 150 euros" and cites a page. The page says "up to 150 euros, depending on the size of the company." What is the problem?
options: None, the number matches.
The answer dropped a condition the page states.
The page is too short to be a source.
The assistant should have linked two pages.

practice.instructions: Write a research question for an AI search assistant, then describe how you would check two of its citations.

rubric.description: The question names the topic, place or time frame instead of asking for a general overview.
The prompt asks for a link or reference for each claim.
The learner opens the source, finds the sentence and compares numbers, dates or conditions.

lessons.goal: Ask an AI tool to answer only from documents you provide, with quotes and page references, and name what it cannot see.
lessons.title: Work from your own documents

blocks.title: Answers from your files
blocks.body: Source-grounded notebooks and chat assistants with file upload can answer from documents you give them, such as a contract, a policy or a set of reports. The answer should come from your files, not from memory.

blocks.title: Ask for quotes and pages
blocks.body: Add rules to your question: "Use only the uploaded files. Quote the exact sentence and give the page. If the files do not say, answer 'not in the documents.'" Then compare each quote with the page.

blocks.title: Know the blind spots
blocks.body: The tool sees only what you uploaded. Scanned pages, images, tables and charts may be read badly or skipped. Long files may be used only in part. Upload confidential files only if your company approves the tool.

blocks.question: You upload three vendor contracts and ask about the notice period. Which instruction best limits invention?
options: Tell me the usual notice period for vendors.
Use only these files. Quote the clause and page. If it is missing, say so.
Summarize everything you know about contracts.
Answer in one word.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What may a grounded tool miss in your uploads?
options: Text inside scanned images.
Numbers in complex tables.
A document you forgot to upload.
Plain text paragraphs in a readable file.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt safest.
blocks.prompt: Which deadlines are in the attached grant guidelines? ___
options: Add typical deadlines if they are missing.
List each deadline with an exact quote and page. If none is stated, write 'not in the documents.'
Give me a short and friendly answer.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A tool that answers from your files can still misquote them.
If the answer is "not in the documents," the topic is not covered anywhere.
Asking for page references makes checking faster.
You can upload any client file to any tool.

blocks.question: The tool quotes "payment within 30 days" and cites page 4. Page 4 says "payment within 14 days." What do you conclude?
options: Page 4 is probably a typo.
The quote is wrong, so do not use the answer.
Both numbers are acceptable.
The tool is right because it read the whole file.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that limits the tool to your documents, asks for quotes and pages, and says what to do when the answer is missing.

rubric.description: The prompt says to use only the provided documents.
The prompt requires exact quotes and page references.
The prompt gives a fallback answer and the learner names a blind spot, such as scans or tables.

lessons.goal: Separate facts from AI interpretation, handle sources that disagree and write a brief where every claim has a source.
lessons.title: Turn facts into a sourced brief

blocks.title: Facts and interpretation
blocks.body: A fact comes from a source: "The report states turnover rose 8%." Interpretation is the AI's reading: "This suggests customers are happier." Ask the assistant to label each statement as fact with source, or interpretation. Keep interpretation only if you agree and mark it as yours.

blocks.title: When sources disagree
blocks.body: Two sources give different numbers. Do not let the assistant average them. Ask it to list both, with date, author and method. Often one is newer, covers a different group or measures something else. If you cannot tell, report the range and say so.

blocks.title: The sourced brief
blocks.body: Write a short brief: one-sentence conclusion, three to five claims, each followed by its source. Delete any claim you could not verify. Ask the assistant to flag sentences without a source, then check them yourself.

blocks.question: Which sentence is an interpretation, not a fact?
options: The survey covered 400 teachers.
Absence rose from 4% to 6%, according to the HR report.
The rise shows that morale is falling.
The report was published in spring.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Two sources give different market sizes. What should you ask?
options: Which source is newer?
Do they measure the same group or definition?
What method did each one use?
Which number is easier to remember?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most useful.
blocks.prompt: Here are my notes and two sources. Draft a brief for my manager. ___
options: Make it sound convincing.
Put the source after every claim and label any sentence that is your interpretation.
Add extra statistics to strengthen it.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: When two sources disagree, you should report both and explain the difference.
A claim you could not verify can stay if it sounds reasonable.
Asking the assistant to flag unsourced sentences helps your review.
An average of two conflicting figures is a safe compromise.

blocks.question: Your draft brief has a strong sentence with no source. What is the best step?
options: Keep it, because the tone fits the brief.
Find a source for it, or delete it.
Cite the AI assistant as the source.
Move it to the end where it is less noticeable.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that turns your sources into a short brief with a source for every claim, and explain how you would handle a conflict.

rubric.description: The prompt requires a source after each claim and a flag on any unsourced sentence.
The prompt asks the assistant to label interpretation separately from facts.
The learner compares date, scope or method of the sources and plans to verify before sharing.

courses.title: Safe AI at Work
courses.description: Decide what you can paste into an AI tool, remove identifying details before you prompt, and follow clear rules for responsible AI use at work.

lessons.goal: Sort your work information into four categories and decide which tool, if any, may receive it.
lessons.title: Know what you are pasting and where

blocks.title: Personal tool or company tool
blocks.body: A free personal AI account and a company-provided tool can look identical. Behind the screen, settings and contracts differ: what is stored, who can read it, and whether it helps train the service. You cannot see this in the chat window. Use the tools your company approves for work.

blocks.title: Four kinds of information
blocks.body: **Public:** already published, such as your website copy. **Internal:** meant for staff, such as a meeting agenda. **Confidential:** harmful if leaked, such as pricing, contracts or financials. **Personal data:** anything about an identifiable person, such as names, addresses or performance reviews. The higher the risk, the fewer tools may receive it.

blocks.title: A real example
blocks.body: A customer complaint names the customer and quotes their address. That is personal data. Do not paste it into a personal tool. In an approved tool, paste it only if your rules allow that category. If unsure, ask before you paste.

blocks.question: What is the most important difference between a personal AI account and a company-approved tool?
options: The approved tool always gives better answers.
Storage and contracts can differ, even if the screen looks the same.
Personal accounts are less accurate, which is the main risk.
There is no difference if you delete the chat afterwards.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which of these are personal data?
options: A customer's home address in an email.
An employee's performance review.
Your company's published opening hours.
A student's grades with their name.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If a tool looks professional, it is safe for confidential documents.
Internal information, such as a staff agenda, should stay out of personal AI accounts.
Information that is already public carries little risk in an AI tool.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this habit safe.
blocks.prompt: Before I paste a document into an AI tool, I ___
options: check that the chat history is turned on.
check what kind of information it contains and whether my company allows it in this tool.
check that it is shorter than a page.

blocks.question: Draft salary bands that only the leadership team has seen are which category?
options: Public
Internal, so any tool is fine
Confidential
No category, because there are no names

practice.instructions: List three kinds of information from your work and sort each into a category, then say which you would never paste into a personal tool.

rubric.description: Each item is placed in a sensible category with a short reason.
Personal or confidential items are identified as not suitable for a personal tool.
Mentions company rules, approved tools or asking a responsible person before pasting.

lessons.goal: Rewrite a text so an AI tool can help without receiving details that identify a person or client.
lessons.title: Anonymize before you prompt

blocks.title: Replace the details
blocks.body: You rarely need real details to get help with wording. Replace names with placeholders like [Client]. Remove IDs and account numbers. Swap exact amounts for [Amount] or a range. Turn dates into "last month". Then add the real details back.

blocks.title: Names are not the only clue
blocks.body: A combination of facts can point to one person without a name. "The only part-time designer in the Northside office who joined last spring" identifies someone. So do a rare job title or a unique event. Look for details only one person or client could match.

blocks.title: A before and after
blocks.body:
Before: "Maria Lopez, account 48213, owes 2,300 and missed the 3 March deadline."

After: "A long-standing client owes [Amount] and missed a recent deadline. Draft a polite reminder."

The task is unchanged. Read your version as a stranger would. Could you guess who it is about? If yes, remove more.

blocks.question: Which version is the safest to paste into a personal AI tool?
options: Draft a reminder to Maria Lopez about invoice 48213.
Draft a reminder to M. L. about her late invoice.
Draft a reminder to a client about a late invoice. Use [Name] and [Amount].
Draft a reminder to the client in apartment 5 about invoice 48213.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which details could still identify someone after the name is removed?
options: Their exact job title in a very small team.
A unique event only they attended.
A general label such as 'a client'.
Their employee ID.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes the prompt safe and still useful.
blocks.prompt: Summarize this complaint and suggest a reply. ___
options: The customer is John Reid from Dock Street.
The customer is [Customer]; the order was [Order] and the amount was [Amount].
The customer is the regular who always orders the oak table on Fridays.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Removing the name is always enough to anonymize a text.
You can add the real details back after the AI gives you a draft.
Rounding an exact amount can reduce what a text reveals.

blocks.question: After anonymizing, what is a good final check?
options: Ask the AI whether it can identify the person.
Read the text as a stranger and see if you could guess who it is about.
Check that every placeholder uses the same brackets.
Check that the text is short.

practice.instructions: Rewrite a realistic work message so it can be pasted safely, then write the prompt you would send.

rubric.description: Names, IDs, exact amounts and exact dates are replaced with placeholders or general wording.
Details that only one person or client could match are removed or generalized.
The final prompt still states what the tool should produce, such as tone and length.

lessons.goal: Apply company rules, decide when to disclose AI use or avoid it, and respond properly when AI output causes a mistake.
lessons.title: Set your own rules for AI at work

blocks.title: Policy first
blocks.body: Your company's rules come before any tip you read. Follow the policy and use only approved tools, even when a personal tool is faster. If you cannot find a policy, ask your manager or IT team. No rule is not the same as permission.

blocks.title: Be open when it matters
blocks.body: Say when AI helped if it affects trust or decisions: client deliverables, assessed work, or anything your rules require. You need not announce every rewritten sentence. If asked, answer honestly. You remain responsible for what you send.

blocks.title: When not to use AI
blocks.body: Do not use AI when rules forbid it, when you cannot remove sensitive details, or to make a decision about a person, such as hiring or grading. A person with authority must decide.

blocks.title: When it goes wrong
blocks.body: If AI output caused a mistake, act quickly. Tell your manager or the affected person, and correct the error. Report accidentally shared sensitive data to whoever handles data at your company.

blocks.question: Your company has no written AI policy. What should you do?
options: Assume it is allowed.
Ask your manager or IT team what is allowed before you use AI for work data.
Use a personal tool, since no rule forbids it.
Wait and see.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. In which situations should you avoid AI or get approval first?
options: Rejecting a candidate based only on an AI summary.
Rewriting a public blog post for tone.
Your policy forbids AI for the client contract you are drafting.
You cannot remove personal data from the text.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: You are responsible for AI-assisted work you send under your name.
You must announce every sentence an AI rephrased.
Fixing a data mistake quietly is better than reporting it.

blocks.question: Pick the best first step after you notice an AI-generated error in a sent report.
blocks.prompt: I will ___
options: wait to see if anyone notices.
tell my manager and the recipient, send a correction and note what happened.
delete the AI chat and say nothing.

blocks.question: A teacher uses AI to draft feedback comments. Which use is appropriate?
options: Let the AI decide each student's final grade.
Use AI to suggest wording, then review the comments and decide the grade yourself.
Paste each student's full name and record into a personal tool.
Send the AI comments without reading them.

practice.instructions: Write a short personal AI rulebook for your work with at least four rules.

rubric.description: At least one rule says to follow company policy or ask when unsure.
Includes when to say AI was used and a situation where AI is not used.
Names concrete steps after an error, such as telling the right person and correcting it.
